253.t: Reeds, mouthpieces and the Albert system clarinet
253.s: Hall describes using medium reeds, only three mouthpieces in his life, and always playing the Albert system.
253.q: No, well, in the old days, you know, it's not like, all your reads now, practically the number now, you see. The old days, you just had to pick out until you get a good one.

253.t: Selma bought in Paris and borrowing a Buffet
253.s: Hall tells how he bought a Selma at the Paris factory during a European tour and borrowed a Buffet from Jimmy Dawson when it cracked.
253.q: Well, I got a, I have a new one, but it's still Albert's system. What make you use? I'm using, well this is the first time I've been using a Selma now for about a year. When we was on this tour in Europe, I bought a Selma, I went to the factory and I bought

253.t: A clarinet on the Mutt Carey recordings
253.s: Hall used an A clarinet once, for the Mutt Carey Scott Joplin rag recordings, and never used C-sharp or E-flat instruments.
253.q: No, I used one A clarinet and that was, I made a recording with, with Mud Carey. You know, about 67 years ago. Yeah, those rags.

253.t: Why Hall plays Albert system rather than Boehm
253.s: Hall tells how the Selma factory owner showed him Boehm clarinets dated 1853, and why he stays with Albert.
253.q: I tell you the experience I had, a lot of people come up to me and ask me why I play an Album System clarinet. So I say well when I started they wasn't making a BAM System clarinet. Well I was wrong, I was just guessing because I had never seen a BAM clarinet before, you see. So, the year before…

253.t: Tone and speed on the Albert clarinet
253.s: Hall argues Albert clarinet has bigger tone for Dixieland; Allen praises Noone's tonguing; Hall's fast Clarinet Marmalade.
253.q: I rather the tone of an Alberts for different bands. Now playing with a combination of six-piece common Dixieland bands, I don't think a BAM clarinet fits in there. Because the tone is beautiful, rich and everything, but it haven't got the big tone when you get, especially when you get in the lower…

253.t: Back to cane: Lavoz reeds and strengths
253.s: After the war Hall returned to cane; he describes the Lavoz brand, its strength grades, and buying by the box. He uses medium hard.
253.q: What to do you do? Yeah, a reed reed. Yeah. Of course now they got a machine that they're making and now you don't have to buy a reed. What number of reeds did you use and what make? Do you don't mind telling? Well, now I'm using a Lavaz. Lavaz. I think the cane actually came from France but the…

253.t: Pros and cons of the plastic reed
253.s: A plastic reed needs no wetting but gave a dead sound that did not cut through, especially on recordings.
253.q: I tell you what was good about it that you didn't have to worry about like a cane reed when you start to play and you had to wet it, especially if you haven't played for a couple of nights, you know? Yeah, yeah. It's dry. You got to wait until you get wet because that particular reed, that plastic…

253.t: Mouthpieces: Myers and grinding the lay
253.s: He has used only three mouthpieces in his life, now a medium-lay Myers, and never ground the lay as some New Orleans players did.
253.q: No, no. I tell you what I have in business. I've been playing kind of, I think I only used three mouthpieces in my whole life. You get a lot of guys that paint these, especially saxophone, the red instrument. Some companies put out all kind of mouthpieces, you know. And they look like they have…

253.t: Ligature placement and a close mouthpiece
253.s: Talk about how Hall puts on the ligature and the effect of a close lay with a soft reed.
253.q: Well, the reason I put mine on there is because usually when you get ready to put that cap on there, and if you're not using it, you'll mess your ears.

253.s: Hall swabs with chamois every night and sometimes oils the instrument.
253.q: I clean my cabinet every night. Every time I get through clean, I dry it out. Just dry it up the swab? Yeah, I swap it out every night.

253.t: Wood, hard rubber and metal clarinets
253.s: Hall prefers solid wood for tone, tried a metal Vegan clarinet, and his wooden Selmer cracked.
253.q: Yeah, the wooden is the best. That way you get a good instrument, and the cheapest instrument, it may be made by the same company, but it's cheaper than the next one. Some of them are made out of hard rubber. But when you get solid wood, you know what I mean? It's better, and the oil of the…

253.t: Wiping the joints and leaving the reed on
253.s: Hall describes his nightly routine of wiping the barrels and mouthpiece and leaving the reed on.
253.q: The only thing like when I take my clarinet out at night, when I get ready to put in the case, I pull it apart. I run that piece of chamois through it. I pull the barrels off, you know, and wipe them on the inside. And I wipe my reeds, I clean my reeds off. I don't take the reed off, but I just…

253.t: How long a reed lasts and trimming it
253.s: A good reed lasts about a month; he sometimes cuts one down, as on his last job with Armstrong.
253.q: Well, that depends. If a good reed will last me, I remember I think I used a reed practically a whole month. A whole month. Even playing almost every night. Yeah. Might last a month. Well, sometimes they're good and then they get real, real damp, real water soaked all the way. Then they get too…

253.t: Burning reeds and plastic reed wear
253.s: Hall describes burning the tip of a reed with a German cap and a coin, and notes plastic reeds chip after about a month.
253.q: Well, I tell you what, I got a cap for, it's German made. I bought the climate just for the ligature. Oh, yeah. You see the cap on your. No, this is too round. See how that mouthpiece, I mean that reed is cut. See if you put it on there, you find out that it's...

253.t: Tempos in the old days and fingering differences
253.s: Hall says old bands never played fast, Tiger Rag the fastest, and he got faster with Teddy Wilson; he compares Albert and Boehm fingering.
253.q: Well now? In the old days? In the old days everything was, every, the hard, let's see, was it. Like Tiger Rags, for instance? Tiger Rags was about the fastest thing they would play. How would they stop it off? It wasn't too fast. But now today I just pick up that, I never could play nothing fast…

253.t: Gutty clarinet tone from the throat
253.s: Russell asks about Hall's strong tone; Hall says it just came naturally and comes from the throat, suiting blues more than ballads.
253.q: I didn't practice anything about it, I don't know, it's just, that's the way, huh? It's just, yeah, it just come to me, I don't, you know what I mean, no, I just picked it up how I did it, I don't know.

124.t: King, Conn, Buescher and Selmer saxophones
124.s: Welburn and McRae sort out which horn he played and discuss the popularity of King, Conn and Buescher, and the arrival of Selmer in 1938.
124.ch: Philadelphia and the McRae Brothers Band, 1908-1929
124.q: Yeah. Well King was too. Because most of your band instruments were King. Must remember mostly all the schools and colleges bought King instruments.

124.t: Saxophone voicings: C melody, E-flat soprano, bass clarinet
124.s: Floyd played C melody; McRae praises the instrument and describes the doubling and the unusual saxophone sound of the band.
124.ch: Philadelphia and the McRae Brothers Band, 1908-1929
124.q: I really couldn't understand the bands today as to why they never used it. Now they used everything -- Now you can understand -- we had -- Guess what we had? We had a bass saxophone, tenor -- that's what I played, tenor -- soprano, and bass clarinet. It was an instrument I played -- just a horn.…

124.t: E-flat soprano, Coon-Sanders, and Rollini as bass sax inspiration
124.s: McRae recalls hearing an E-flat soprano in Detroit with Chick, and Adrian Rollini's bass sax with Coon-Sanders as his inspiration.
124.ch: Philadelphia and the McRae Brothers Band, 1908-1929
124.q: Detroit when we're playing with Chick. The guy had an E-flat soprano. And it's beautiful. It's a wonderful saxophone, but nobody played it.

124.t: Why McRae switched from Conn to Selmer saxophone
124.s: Welburn asks about the switch; McRae says the Conn was too weak to be heard across the packed Savoy.
124.ch: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
124.q: In playing the Savoy, I would notice on a Saturday night or any given big night we had up there, I could be playing that horn and like, from over (Inaudible) to the desk out there, the crowd will be so heavy that you couldn't hear me in the back, you know.

124.t: Trading in the Conn at Manny's and trying the Selmer
124.s: He got a Selmer and Otto Link mouthpiece; the new horn sounded distant until he got used to it.
124.ch: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
124.q: And I'm upstairs and I'm playing the thing and it sounds good. I'm in the room back there, I put my mouthpiece on and it sounds good to me. I say, "Oh, this is nice."

124.s: Webster blew McRae's horn at the Paramount and immediately bought one at Manny's, starting a switch from Conn to Selmer.
124.ch: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
124.q: Now we're playing the Paramount. Ben Webster come back after the second show. Ben Webster come back and say, "I hear you got a Selmer." I say, "Yeah." (Inaudible). "Come up in the dressing room." horn laying right there. There's the Mind if I try this?"

124.t: The Selmer's carrying power at the Kansas City auditorium and Savoy
124.s: McRae recalls not being heard in a crowd of 12,000 with the Conn and being heard clearly with the Selmer.
124.ch: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
124.q: Big sound right around you. I remember when I played with Chick when we played in Kansas City -- what really got me against

124.t: Conn bass sax and rubber mouthpieces
124.s: He liked the Conn bass sax, rarely used baritone, and used rubber mouthpieces before the Link caught on.
124.ch: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
124.q: The bass -- the Conn I liked. But I would've got a bass saxophone, but the Conn was -- The bass was -- they made a real good bass saxophone. And it had a tremendous sound to it.

124.t: Reeds and how he shaved them
124.s: McRae used strength four and a half or five, shaved the length, and favored King reeds.
124.ch: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
124.q: I'll shave it down and, you know, like going towards the front of the reed, you know. Take it towards the back just so it wouldn't --

124.t: Never going back from the Selmer; borrowing and renting horns
124.s: McRae never played anything else after the Selmer, and a name band member could borrow or rent a horn easily.
124.ch: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
124.q: Well, if you are travelling especially in a big band, you have no trouble getting a horn. If you're in town and somebody got a horn, they would lend you a horn, or something like that, if you (inaudible) go to the store and get a horn. Plus you're with a big band. You're with Chick or you're with…

124.t: The first night with the Selmer
124.s: McRae sweated through a set because he could not hear the new horn, but the sound carried out front.
124.ch: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
124.q: Called it the "run around," you know. Wind up went out and bought him a snare and went on the bass drum. (humming notes) (Inaudible). So when Selmer came out with this big ad with Coleman Hawkins, every tenor player -- A lot of guys (Inaudible), they couldn't play that. But once I picked it up, I…

124.t: The Link mouthpiece for tenor soloists
124.s: Tenor men used Link mouthpieces to cut above the brass, while altos mostly stayed with rubber ones.
124.ch: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
124.q: Whatchamacallem used that mouthpiece I was trying to tell you about now. He used a rubber mouthpiece. It was a very good mouthpiece. But the rubber mouthpiece -- the Link was mostly for the tenor men that had to do a lot of honking. You know, playing really. You know, that was a good mouthpiece for…

124.t: Carrying reeds on the road; Vido Musso takes the sixes
124.s: He travelled with several boxes of reeds, and Vido Musso walked off with three boxes of number sixes.
124.ch: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
124.q: boxes of reeds. Because if I'm going on the road anywhere for like three months or I'm going to be out there for a little while, I got to play theater dates, I go down to -- get me a half a dozen boxes.

124.t: Heat on the road and caring for horns
124.s: In Texas and Oklahoma heat the reeds cracked; they used wet towels, oiled pads, and later enjoyed the Selmer's built-in springs.
124.ch: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
124.q: : Yeah. In Texas the weather was so hot and Oklahoma. It was like all0 at night -- in the daytime. Like when we get to the ballroom, it'll be like 100, you know, 90 and we play in shirt sleeves. It be (inaudible), you know. And Jeff and I, we used to put a glass of water down on the side. And when…

124.t: Chick Webb features bass sax and "By-Heck"
124.s: Coleman Hawkins also played bass sax; Chick Webb got McRae a Henderson arrangement and let him trade breaks on "By-Heck".
124.ch: Philadelphia and the McRae Brothers Band, 1908-1929
124.q: Coleman had a -- Chick finally got this arrangement from Fletcher for me. It was a thing -- I forget the name of it. I was all for bass saxophone.

198.t: Trying the 13-key Henry Gunkel clarinet and plastic-coated reeds
198.s: The visitors bring a 13-key clarinet marked Henry Gunkel; Emile finds wood has a better tone and tries a plastic-coated reed.
198.q: That's to stop it from soaking. I suppose, something like that. Yeah, to stop it from the water from soaking in. It does hold up quite a bit longer.

198.s: Asked about the mouthpiece on the clarinet Russell got from him, Emile says he dislikes small mouthpieces and likes a bigger one.
198.q: Yeah, yeah. Why, too? You see, I don't know. I believe I got a mouthpiece on that other clarinet. That I never used. Uh-huh. It's a little mouthpiece, you know? Uh-huh. And I don't like a little mouthpiece. I like a bigger mouthpiece.

198.t: Fingering: side keys and his own faster fingering
198.s: They discuss the side key and alternate fingerings; Emile prefers his untrained first-and-third finger method as faster.
198.q: Yeah, now and then. A different scene that you can't get by with. So that would be the C sharp key or what would that be? Right here.

198.t: Emile's own old clarinets and offers to repair them
198.s: Emile shows his locked case and unused spare clarinet; the interviewer offers to recork and repad it, and Emile says he likes old instruments for tone.
198.q: I lost it all right, but I lost it for years ago, see, this key. But this is all, that's a lock right there. It had a trigger on it, you know? Oh, yeah.

198.t: How many clarinets he has owned
198.s: Emile guesses he has had more than ten clarinets, around three in A and six or seven in B-flat.
198.q: Yeah, for the Bs I had, I run into about three A's. For the Bs, I don't know, I run into about six or seven Bs. Yeah. Yeah. I rode all my carers.

198.t: When the saxophone arrived in New Orleans
198.s: Barnes says clarinetists like Kaiser did not play saxophone, and the saxophone came to the city late, with Big Eye Louis bringing one back.
198.q: No, no, they just clarinet. Well I'm telling you saxophone just came out here a couple of years ago, you know. But saxophone was a sign. Well saxophone was an offense when you see what Joe Allen and Sheldon Sten and Mads had sax and Mads from Williams but they had good clarinet players. But they…

198.t: Barnes's clarinets and wooden versus hard rubber mouthpieces
198.s: Barnes and the interviewers work out which clarinets he owned and what mouthpieces he used, including how he filed them open; Raymond Burke sandpapers his.
198.q: wooden one that no i let's see no i think that the one was with the first one it came before the other one one behind that window before that you know you had another one before that i had one before that but it was the winner another way with it yeah yeah but it was all cut up from the teeth

198.t: 13-key versus 15-key clarinets and the tone of wood versus rubber
198.s: Barnes says early clarinets mostly had 13 keys, calls the instrument delicate, and prefers the tone of old wooden clarinets over rubber or metal.
198.q: no i think it was the 13 we hardly had any 15 key car yeah yeah yeah 15 key key car that was a long time after yeah that's a good after that's a different in uh in the 15 and uh and uh 20th now you understand it's a big difference they change they operate and more and more yeah they seem to be…

198.t: Reeds: cutting stiff cane reeds and switching to a plastic reed
198.s: Barnes describes how an older clarinetist cut his reeds extra stiff, where he buys reeds, and his difficult change to a long-lasting plastic reed.
198.ch: Big Eye Louis and Barnes's own playing
198.q: Well he's reed I couldn't blow it, but I cut my reed right now to two or two and a half. See I don't use any one or one and a half reed, I couldn't use it in my life.

198.t: Parades and pitching a B flat clarinet
198.s: He played parades with most bands, never used E flat, and describes adjusting joints of a B flat clarinet to pitch any key.
198.q: I never used an E flat. I used a B flat. It was a... E flat, I had an E flat and I gave it away. I don't know if they many men use E flat now. Most of them are playing with B flat. Of course, when I was playing in Scotch music I used a B. I had A and B and then time we used A and B. I used a B and…

198.t: Low-register playing with a derby mute
198.s: Allen recalls the Charlie Love record session; Barnes explains his low-register clarinet played into a felt derby, which no one else did until his records.
198.q: That's all my home. That's all my home. Low right of stone. They can take the low register. And uh, the door that's covered as a man trumpet, cover the trumpet. You got a way down on bass baritone tone on there. Way deep. It's a joy. You can probably feel the joy on the floor if you're sitting…

198.t: Two clarinets in a band and clarinet with saxophone
198.s: Asked about two-clarinet bands, Barnes says it was done only occasionally; the clarinet should lead and a tenor saxophone could play variations.
198.q: Well I don't remember nothing about that. I don't know nothing about that. And I know plenty of musicians and music too. You see I don't say I know music, but I know some of them. You certainly know more than most people. Yeah, but in the meantime for clarinets to do that, they can put two…

198.t: Clarinet parts on High Society and Picou
198.s: Solos were tune-specific parts such as the clarinet part in High Society, which Barnes says is strangled today. Picou praised his playing and sat in at a party.
198.q: Well, the only solo that we made in them days, it was F. U. Harry to make, but not no special solo. You know, this is like what tune called for the Clowns part we make it. Trumblet part he'd make it, Trumblet part he'd make it. Like Hot Society or something like that. Yeah, yeah. All tunes like…

198.t: Rough and growling clarinet: Lorenzo Tio
198.s: Asked who played rough, Barnes names the younger Tio with his heavy reed, whom he says could get rough though he sounds smooth on records.
198.q: They played all that music. It's more in parts I think. It's a musician, you know? Mm-hmm. They worked as a musician. It didn't work as a musician. It didn't work as a musician. Like I would work. You wouldn't call him hot? Well he was all right.

0.t: Albert system versus Boehm system clarinet
0.s: He stayed with the Albert system clarinet, which he thought allowed free passages and a distinct tone that the Boehm could not.
0.ch: National Guard band and first jobs in Chicago
0.q: And eventually, when I went into the Army band -- the National Guard, then you had a choice of switching over to the Boehm system.

0.t: Buying a first saxophone and leaving it with Johnny Dodds
0.s: Clarinet devotees disliked the saxophone; he left his first alto with Johnny Dodds before leaving Chicago for New York.
0.ch: Coleman Hawkins, Bernie Young and doubling on tenor
0.q: MR. CALDWELL: And Johnny (unintelligible) taken it and he'd play it for about two months, say, you come on and get your saxophone. I said, all right, but, I said, I thought you were going to play the thing. It still wasn't played. But (by) that time I was ready to there moderator could leave…

0.t: Meeting Coleman Hawkins and Hawk's cello and clarinet
0.s: Hawkins heard Caldwell's clarinet style in Chicago and invited him to join; they discuss Hawkins's cello training and why Caldwell settled on tenor.
0.ch: Coleman Hawkins, Bernie Young and doubling on tenor
0.q: Then Hawk came through before I left with Mamie, slap tonguing and I got stuck playing with the tenor. Hawk was (unin- telligible). He was crazy about my clarinet style. I said-- he said to me, said, hey, say, why don't you come on and join us? I said, well, Hawk --

0.t: The 1923 Bernie Young recording and Stump Evans's C-melody
0.s: Personnel of the 1923 record; Stump Evans, from Kansas City, played C-melody, which people mistook for alto, and Hawkins asked about him.
0.ch: Coleman Hawkins, Bernie Young and doubling on tenor
0.q: '23. First I (unintelligible) we started with because we skipped (unintelligible), but Bernie Young on Mike McKendrick trumpet, Mack Hendricks on guitar, Preston Jackson on trombone.

0.t: Alto players who switched to tenor and Caldwell's doubling
0.s: Discussion of Lester Young and others who began on alto; Caldwell doubled tenor and baritone with Arthur Gibbs's band and could pick up alto.
0.ch: Coleman Hawkins, Bernie Young and doubling on tenor
0.q: Really would, because I used to double for -- from the B flat tenor to the E flat baritone saxophone, like with Arthur Gibbs band. And Benny Carter (said, you play) alto wanted -- fine also. I could pick up the alto and play it. you an unshy fellow, and I said why He said (unintelligible), said,…

0.t: Giving up clarinet for tenor; doubling clarinet and soprano
0.s: He stopped playing clarinet as a feature when he stayed on tenor with Cliff Jackson, though section parts required clarinet and soprano.
0.ch: Charlie Johnson, Willie Gant and the late 1920s
0.q: That's when it happened. I didn't go back on alto any more. We used to play the clarinet together if you were a saxophone player, down there because at that time at a place you had to play clarinet.

0.t: Pipe and straight soprano saxophones; Hodges and Bechet
0.s: There are two kinds of soprano sax; Hodges played it like Bechet and shared Caldwell's birthday.
0.ch: Charlie Johnson, Willie Gant and the late 1920s
0.q: Well, you know, the soprano is a peculiar instrument. A lot of people don't know it, but there are two different sopranos. The pipe model and the straight model --

0.t: Elmer Snowden's band at Small's, and Garvin Bushell's many instruments
0.s: Snowden picked good players; Garvin Bushell, first seen in Chicago with Lucille Hegamin, played oboe, flute and bassoon and the band played overture excerpts at intermission.
0.ch: Small's Paradise, Fletcher Henderson and Horace
0.q: Yeah. He had a very good (unintelligible) picking musicians and got the band he wanted. And Cliff was very nice too about it. Well, them fellows, you know, they brought up in (unintelligible) from the old school coming up, the old fellows would --

0.t: Ben Webster switches from a Conn to a Selmer saxophone
0.s: Caldwell coached Webster through the unfamiliar Selmer, whose tone carries farther than it sounds under the player's ear.
0.ch: Benny Carter, saxophones and Coleman Hawkins's last years
0.q: He said, Selmer. Well, the Selmer's peculiar instrument. If not like the Conn, the Conn you -- when you play it, (unintelligible) you could hear it right on top of you, but when you're playing the Selmer, you're supposed to think you're playing loud, but the tone goes, has the carrying power.…

0.t: Why players moved to Selmer, and Caldwell's current horn
0.s: Most players switched to Selmer; Caldwell bought a new Selmer before the Denmark trip.
0.ch: Benny Carter, saxophones and Coleman Hawkins's last years
0.q: Selmer's did. Selmer's a beautiful instrument because everything is underneath your fingers, the execution, get tone out of it.

0.s: Caldwell never had mouthpiece trouble; the section with Arthur Gibbs began using metal mouthpieces in 1927 and Hawkins did too.
0.ch: Benny Carter, saxophones and Coleman Hawkins's last years
0.q: Well, Hawk -- we were -- when the Berg Larson -- not the Berg Larson in -- it was the fellow, the first reed section we'd had up to Savoy with Arthur Gibbs. All of us started using the other metal mouth- piece (unintelligible) in New York later. And Hawk started to using them, and we all started to…

0.t: Hawkins's reeds and the development of his sound
0.s: Hawk used hard reeds, number three and a half or four; Dance feels his sound grew stronger over the years.
0.ch: Benny Carter, saxophones and Coleman Hawkins's last years
0.q: Yes, he did, because being (unintelligible), Hawk, what you using? He said, using number three and a half or four. That's stiff. I used to use the three. But then the mouthpiece was open. You had to use a (unintelligible) soft reed. But he had that volume, and he used them three, three and a half.…

0.t: Chu Berry picks up the tenor at the Colonnades
0.s: At the Colonnades with Fat Man Turner's Arcadians, Chu Berry filled in on tenor when the tenor player did not show and kept it.
0.q: Chu was playing alto. Chu was working down at the Colonnades when I was down there with -- with Arthur Gibbs, and Fat Man Turner, the bass player, had taken the band into the Colonnades.

0.t: Multi-instrumentalists: George Dixon and doublers who play many horns
0.s: Dixon played alto and baritone beautifully; players who take up many horns rarely play any one well.
0.ch: Pay, the Fletcher Henderson circle and later life
0.q: Well, you know, some of them people are some people that -- some people can do these kind of things that they're versatile at.

724.t: Why the clarinet and his attitude to saxophone
724.s: He took up clarinet because he loved it; he owned a soprano sax briefly and others like Barnes and George Lewis dislike saxophone.
724.q: Do you have a play saxophone? No. Would you play one if somebody gave you one? I don't know because it might throw me back on that outer system clarinet. That's why I never bought everybody. You never even owned a saxophone? Well, I bought one. I bought a soprano.

724.s: He played B-flat clarinet with Eureka for about a year, ignoring E-flat parts.
724.q: No, I don't. We didn't talk about the Eureka Heart at all. No. You were with them, I know, around 44 or 45, because you were in that book of jazz ways. Yeah. Yeah, I was with them a while. I don't know. I don't know. I don't know. I imagine about a year.

724.t: Old clarinetists and biting the mouthpiece versus lip embouchure
724.s: Discussion of the Tios, Big Eye and others, and whether to bite the mouthpiece or cover the teeth with the lip; Burbank uses the lip.
724.q: Well, I don't know, but I do believe this, that the majority of them bite their lip because I was told that that was the right way. There's only one man that I do know that used to bite the mouthpiece, and from playing the horn, from playing the horn a lot, his teeth cut a gutter in the mouthpiece,…

724.s: Burbank thinks Alexander played the Albert system back then.
724.ch: Childhood, Mardi Gras and first brass band
724.q: I don't believe, I... I don't believe. I think he used to play the album system.

724.t: E-flat clarinet and number of keys on old clarinets
724.s: He tried an E-flat clarinet and disliked it; they discuss key counts and rings on older Albert system clarinets.
724.q: I had gotten one and it needed a pan and I took it and kind of fixed it up and blow it on it and I didn't like it. It's so high. Yeah. And I just put it down.

724.t: Albert system versus Boehm and his current clarinet
724.s: He plays a French clarinet, prefers the Albert system and thinks the Boehm tone is less good.
724.q: Well, I've been trying to locate a summer or a Buffet and I still would like to have one in Albert's system. Yeah, hard to find now.

724.t: Getting a big tone and reed strength
724.s: He says players use too soft a reed; he uses a number three.
724.q: Is it something about peace? I think the main trouble is that they use too soft a reed.

724.t: Mouthpieces: filing, H1S versus H2S and a stolen mouthpiece
724.s: Filed-down mouthpieces are ruined; he describes his H1S and a stolen Selmer mouthpiece.
724.q: Well, that's the mistake they made, they ruined them. I have a couple of mouthpiece that that fellas ruined like that, that I got, and I couldn't blow them. A couple of mouthpiece that they ruined like that, file them down. Them mouthpiece comes by numbers. You can buy them open.

724.t: Plastic reeds and soaking cane reeds
724.s: He rejects plastic reeds and explains how he wets reeds and sets them slightly below the tip.
724.q: to play, I couldn't get anything out of it. As long as I'd play, as long as I'd finger low, it'd be alright. When I'd try to make a high note, it would close on me. And I was told from someone that used the plastic reed, that after you get used to the plastic reed, you wouldn't be able to use the…

724.s: Too closed a facing flops, too open wastes wind; they discuss trying an H2S.
724.q: Yes, it do. See, too close, when it's closed too much, when you blow hard, it'll close and nothing come out. It'll flop. That's right, yeah.

724.t: Two clarinets in one band; Piku and Neely Barnes
724.s: With two clarinets they made separate variations; Piku wrote him a second part to High Society.
724.q: Well, we didn't play the same, you know, so we'd just go ahead and make all of them. Just make your own variations. Yeah. I don't know.

571.t: Albert system clarinet and a Boehm-mixed instrument
571.s: George says he always played Albert system, once tried Boehm, and had a clarinet his mother bought that mixed both.
571.ch: George Lewis's first bands and instruments
571.q: I never saw them until the 80 years. I wouldn't say they weren't playing, you know, but I never saw them until the 80 years. Because I get, somewhere or another I get confused. I was in some of those, yeah. But I did have, I had a crown that my mother had got me in the 20s, which was part Albert…

571.s: Lewis says he never used another player's clarinet and always needs his own mouthpiece.
571.q: No, I'll tell you, I never knew about a carinet. I couldn't blow any barcane. I'd have to sit on your hands. And, uh, I'm not afraid to catch that. I just been, I just been, I just been really, a lot of other men, like myself, using rubber. Uh, my feet might be not strong enough for you to come out…

571.t: Clarinet cracking, metal versus wood tone, Harry Pedler clarinet
571.s: He explains how clarinets crack and are repaired, and says he finds little tonal difference between metal and wood, naming the Harry Pedler clarinet.
571.q: Yeah, that's the one I, I used the other night to crack. Well, they tell you, if a clarinet don't crack, it's no good. The grain, you see. So, uh, the weather will crack. I've gotten the one I have now. What I use the other night is, uh, it's got a steel, a metal, two, see. And two metal rings…

571.t: Mouthpiece lay, reeds, and his father's goat-horn reed
571.s: Talk of mouthpiece lay and matching soft reeds to wide lays; Lewis's father tried to make a reed from goat horn.
571.q: I would like a wide layer. A wide layer, I could use a soft reed. A bind is bind with the mouthpiece. If you've got a close reed, you use a hard mouthpiece. Try to slide. Yeah, the layer you use a hard reed. If you've got a wide layer, use a soft reed.

571.t: How long reeds last, trimming and burning them
571.s: He describes reed lifespan, his habit of cutting reeds with a coin and a match, and views on reed cutters.
571.q: You get wet, you go outside, you know. You don't want to pay the driver off. You don't want to pay the driver off. But, um, somebody had to pay the driver off. it's no good. Outside just scraping. I don't like scraping. Because you're going to get it too soft. So I already used a new read. For the…

571.t: Wood, rubber and metal clarinets compared
571.s: He prefers wood, compares rubber, and relays Bill Russell's remark that material makes no tonal difference; his museum clarinet was out of line.
571.q: I like a wooden clarinet the best. But before I got this, this ram system, I used it as rubber clarinet. I got the same thing out of the rubber clarinet as I did the wood. But the wood, it gets better. Because you're not, if you drop the rubber, you know, that's not a very tall, ever. You put half…

571.t: Albert versus Boehm keys and technique
571.s: Discussion of simple Albert, Boehm system being easier, Raymond Burke's rubber bands on keys, and use of side keys.
571.q: Because I got two clarinetes. It's a different thing. The BIM system is much easier to play. Yeah, well, you can see all the Mardi Gras Fairees and all the school bands and music. You never see nobody wearing alberts. Now they don't make alberts in the state, no more. But before when they were…

571.t: How George Lewis came to own Jimmie Noone's clarinet
571.s: Lewis explains that a Los Angeles music store lent him a clarinet that had belonged to Jimmie Noone, and he ended up buying it. It is the Selmer he still plays; he places this about 1955-56.
571.q: Well, my client and I had a rubber, a foil rubber client and it fell and it broke a piece off the ring. I brought it to the millage store in Los Angeles, on Vine Street. And asked them, could they fix it? See, they could fix it, but I wanted to borrow one for the work. They didn't have any album…

571.t: First E-flat clarinet and an all-day parade
571.s: George recalls playing E-flat clarinet for the first time on an all-day parade and how he got the instrument.
571.ch: George Lewis's first bands and instruments
571.q: But yeah, I learned there was another Eureka band in the early days in this band. Probably he was in that band. Might have been in that. But this band here, I'm telling you about this, it's the first time I ever played E-flat clarinet in my life. And we played the second to the last All Fellas Day…

641.t: Dr. Moon hires him; the special bus and the saxophone
641.s: Dr. Moon's medicine show offered him a job and bought him a saxophone; he describes the bus with vats, the company, and the 1926 date.
641.q: And finally, uh, a medicine show came through Opelousa's, Dr. Moon. That's what you hear me talking about all the time. So, Dr. Moon offered me a job. He wanted me to play a saxophone and clarinet. So, Dr. Moon bought me a saxophone. Cause I didn't have no room.

641.s: Joe describes his first ebonite clarinet, the Conn Albert System his father ordered, and why he thinks the Albert has better tone.
641.ch: Instruments, first jobs and the regional scene
641.q: It was an Albert System. My first clarinet was an old clarinet that was a hard rubber piece; they made them out of ebonite, they called it.

641.t: His Albert clarinet in the New Orleans museum
641.s: Joe switched to Boehm in 1950 and regrets it; he lent his old Albert to Doc Souchon's museum and could not get it back.
641.ch: Instruments, first jobs and the regional scene
641.q: clarinet is in... I've got a clarinet in the museum in New Orleans that they show, the Museum Hall of Fame that just opened, and it was a special-made Selmer clarinet Albert System. It used to belong to a musician that played with the New York Symphony. I got it through a fellow in Seattle that I…

641.t: Buying a ninety-nine dollar saxophone; costume, singing and dancing
641.s: Doc Moon bought Joe a Conn alto sax in Lafayette to be repaid at two dollars a week, and Joe asked for a Six Brown Brothers style costume and added singing and dancing.
641.q: Well, the smaller the town is, the more they would cost you, you know. If I went to Baton Rouge maybe or New Orleans, I could probably have got one a little cheaper than that.

641.s: Joe says Picou's clarinet was made with an upturned bell, like a saxello, and Joe was the only one he let touch it.
641.q: No. I was the only that could ever touch that clarinet, I'll tell you that. They put out another thing a lot similar to that thing called a saxello.

641.t: Dropping the clarinet for alto sax; still owing Doc Moon
641.s: Joe fell in love with the alto sax and let his clarinet go, still owing Doc Moon ninety dollars and hoping to find a circus in Billboard.
641.ch: Southern Illinois roadhouse and St. Louis
641.q: Yes, I practically got off the clarinet. But to tell you the truth, I fell in love with the saxophone. At that time, people loved saxophone.

641.t: Learning the slap-tongue and Yellow Dog Blues
641.s: Joe slap-tongued on the spur of the moment in Santa Barbara, having been inspired by a twelve-year-old clarinetist years earlier, and Ory refused to record Yellow Dog Blues.
641.ch: Gene Mayl, Teddy Buckner and the Dixie Flies
641.q: No. And I don't know why these things come to you. This tune, "The Sugar Blues," the trumpet would have a solo on it, and in the middle of it was a break. And I would take a low-register solo in "The Sugar Blues." So we was playin' a concert in Santa Barbara, and it just came to me, "When I get to…

641.t: Quarrel with Martel, marriage to Hillary, and hired by Doc Moon
641.s: After a falling out with Old Man Martel, whose daughter Hillary he married, Joe borrowed an alto sax in Opelousas, auditioned and was hired at twenty-one dollars a week.
641.q: Well, yeah, of course! That's what I'm coming to. He didn't travel across the nation, but we went as far as Ohio and Illinois. We went through Arkansas when we left Louisiana. Anyway, it was a bootlegging joint. It was Prohibition, and I was in there getting a drink... I was working in the Martel…

629.s: He has played both and prefers the Albert system for tone and ease.
629.q: That's what I'm using now. Albert. Yes, I know that.

629.t: Playing High Society without keys; reeds
629.s: He explains he mostly plays on the holes, plays High Society with no keys, and scrapes his reeds with a knife.
629.q: Nothing but holes. God, join me in them holes. Them things there. Yeah. His finger's right there. Yeah. His finger's right there.

629.t: Mouthpiece, the French clarinet and its barrel
629.s: He has used only one mouthpiece his whole life, and describes the clarinet given him by a music store, from France, that was offered $1,500.
629.q: the the the music store made me a present of that clarinet. And he got it from from France. From France. That's what I got now. From France. And there's nobody to touch that. It's a nice find, eh? I was offered $1,500 for it.

629.t: The E-flat clarinet and parade playing
629.s: He explains the E-flat clarinet, its straight bell and smaller mouthpiece; an interviewer recalls hearing him in a parade with Old Man Barbarin on alto horn.
629.q: we don't want to keep you very long because i know you want to get some rest again yeah okay but um is there anything else that you can think of ralph that we might ask i guess

629.t: Albert-system versus Boehm clarinet and embouchure
629.s: Picou prefers the Albert clarinet for jazz because it has fewer keys; talk of tone and where to put the teeth.
629.q: Did you ever play the Bame System Clarinet or always the Albert? Oh, yeah. I played both of them. You played both of them? Yeah. But already Albert. Why do you like the Albert better? Yeah, because Albert for jazz is more easy than the band. Because the band has got too much keys. And the Albert,…

629.s: Picou talks about the E-flat clarinet in brass bands, mouthpiece alterations, and using number three reeds scraped with glass.
629.q: I'm not a man. That's not a big one. I'm not a man. I'm not a man. I'm not a man. I'm not a man. I'm a man. I'm a man. Lero. Is there much difference in playing the E-flat clarinet? Do you play it? No, sir. Is it hard to blow? Gee. It just one, this closer finger. Closer fingering. That's all. In a…

629.t: His clarinet and its curved bell
629.s: Picou describes his French-made Albert-system clarinet with a curved bell.
629.q: I don't remember. I was going to ask a bit more about your clarinet. What make is your clarinet? Is it a... Algar. Algar system. I mean, is it made in France or... Yeah, I remember. Yeah, one is in France. You don't remember the maker of it now. Is it Buffet or who made it? It has that peculiar...…

629.t: Advice to young clarinet students and embouchure
629.s: Picou tells students to keep lips firm, and says he only ever covered the bottom teeth.
629.q: Well, I tell them whether you... When you're blowing a clarinet, don't do this. Just puff out your cheeks and all of them. Yeah. Because something is in your mouth, you do this. Yeah. Keep your lips back there firm. Yeah. Yeah.

307.t: Tone, stiff reeds and playing without teeth
307.s: He finds a bigger tone on the Boehm, uses a stiff reed and a strong lip, and has long played without teeth, struggling to play with dentures.
307.q: I think it's easier to play louder and bigger tone. Because you have much more keys to make some different notes, I think. That, that's a, might be a different on that.

307.t: Mouthpiece and blowing softer on the Boehm
307.s: He used the mouthpiece that came with the Boehm clarinet and found he must blow softer or it squeaks; he returned George Lewis's silver Albert.
307.q: No, the blow is softer because I noticed when I blew hard, it would make false noise. Yeah, yeah. It would make a plain sound. I've noticed that myself.

307.t: Saxophone worries, Leblanc and a horn bought via Larry Barbarin
307.s: He fears sax would hurt his clarinet lip, is told about Leblanc clarinets, and recalls buying a French clarinet through Larry Barbarin.
307.q: You'll lose your lip for your clarinet, yes. Well that's what I could be afraid of. Yeah you don't want to do that. No I sure wouldn't want to do that because uh clarinet is the thing that kept me going all these years years. Of course one time ago I had to count on these smaller bands but since uh…

307.t: Rubber bands on clarinets; giving an Albert to Handy
307.s: They discuss clarinetists who held keys with rubber bands, and Thomas gave his last Albert to Handy while recalling John Lewis and Piku trying Boehm.
307.q: No not that I know of. No. Did it? No. It didn't have a lot of rubber bands. Don's boy used to carry a lot of rubber bands. It was just Ernest Mowier. Oh yeah. Oh boy he died not long ago. Yeah. Well he used to have a lot of rubber bands on his clarinet. I really, every time he'd see it. Of course…

307.s: He now owns three Boehm clarinets: a Regent, a Noble bought from Peterson, and one in a Leblanc case.
307.ch: Other bands: Royal Jazz, H&J, Rainbow Room
307.q: Yes. Uh, this other clarinet. Now, let me see if that's the one I bought by Peterson or the one I got from, uh, well, I guess it matters. It don't matter which place I got it from. It's Noble. Noble. Noble, yes. Oh, Noble. Yeah. Never heard of that. That's a, that's a BEM you're speaking about.…

307.t: Cane reeds, homemade trimming and caulk grease
307.s: He uses cane reeds, trims them with nickels, a cigarette and a razor blade, buys at Peterson, and learned about caulk grease.
307.q: I never did play a plastic reed yet. The boys told me about it. Why don't I get a plastic reed? But I never did. Because sometimes they're alright and most of the time they're not. They cost more and all. They last longer. But I always feel like they may not blow right to me. Where there was reeds…

307.t: Reed strengths: Peterson on numbers, choosing a three and a half
307.s: Peterson explained reed numbering, Thomas settled on three and a half for tone, and rejects advice to drop to two and a half.
307.q: It was a softer reed because after, I believe Peterson was, when I started buying reeds from him, he asked me what number you want. I said number. I said number.

307.t: The clarinets he has owned; wanting a Selmer
307.s: He has owned six or seven clarinets since his first, plays two Boehm clarinets, bought one from Peterson, and wants a Selmer.
307.q: Yes the same one. The same one. Yes. Oh that sounds good. Yeah. Uh uh but since that I bought another band system since that though. Oh yeah? Yeah well I played both of them now. Oh I see you take two out now. Two out yeah well I might leave one home for two three months play the other one and then…

9.t: Playing soprano or alto freely, and C.B. Conn saxophones
9.s: He liked Russell's band best because he could choose soprano or alto; he played a Conn soprano and alto and had little regard for Selmers.
9.ch: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
9.q: I enjoyed working in Russell's band more than any band I ever worked with. At ease, you know what I mean? No restraint there at all or nothin'.

9.s: Cole played beautifully but threw away reed after reed, never satisfied, which Holmes teased him about.
9.q: : Oh, yeah, with the reeds. Oh yeah. Well, he would play something, and it would be so beautiful. You'd just sit back and look at him with admiration. He was playing so beautiful and with such ease, you know. and then, when he gets through, he tears the reed off the horn and throws it away, and…

9.t: Number-two reeds, and a trumpeter friend's too-stiff clarinet reed
9.s: Holmes used medium reeds to hear resonance, and a trumpet-playing friend's stiff reed gave no resonance on his new clarinet.
9.q: No, I was mentioning that because there was a fellow here the other day, he's a trumpet player, so he says... I mean, he is a trumpet player, who has ...(?)...(?) And he's taking up clarinet now. He's about two years older than I am. Now he gets involved with a clarinet. So I told

9.t: Oboe reeds and Rico number twos
9.s: Oboists make their own double reeds, but Holmes never learned to shave a reed, so he bought boxes of Rico number twos.
9.q: Yeah. Most oboe players, they make their own reeds. Which I never got that far with it. No, I would buy a reed and let it get soft after soaking it, and this-that-and-the-other. I never could shave a reed. I was never successful shaving any kind of a reed. Even saxophone. I never know the right…

9.t: Failing at flute and the stolen soprano
9.s: He never could play flute even on Walton's and Howard Johnson's flutes, and his soprano was stolen from a California club, ending his soprano playing.
9.ch: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
9.q: Oh, yes. I had a flute of my own. And I always figured there was something wrong with the flute, because I couldn't play it. So I sold the flute for ten dollars. And then years later, Greely Walton loaned me his flute, which he had been playing and there was nothing wrong

9.s: He never used the stock mouthpiece, tried every kind of metal and other mouthpiece, and sold two from a drawerful to a player from Machito's band.
9.q: I was more like a... I was more a mouthpiece freak. You know, I've never got a decent mouthpiece. No mouthpiece ever suited me. I was more a mouthpiece freak, and he was a reed freak!

9.t: Saxophonists had to own a clarinet; Buster Bailey's wooden clarinet
9.s: Every saxophonist carried a Boehm clarinet because the stock parts called for it; Buster Bailey impressed him most in the 1925 Henderson band.
9.ch: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
9.q: Sure. Everybody. All saxophone players had clarinets. Everyone couldn't play them. Most of them couldn't. But you had to have it.

9.t: Doubling on clarinet and Howard Johnson and Chu Berry replacing him
9.s: He carried clarinet and soprano in one case, had given up baritone, and left Hill's band when Johnson and Chu Berry came in.
9.ch: Willie Lynch, the Blue Rhythm Band and Teddy Hill
9.q: No. He didn't touch the violin with Teddy. Yeah, he was a great violinist. But he didn't play it with Teddy Hill. He played clarinet and saxophone.

619.t: Freak fingering for C sharp and B flat on the Albert system
619.s: He explains the Albert-system clarinet and the unusual alternate fingerings he learned for C sharp and B flat, and a player who plugged broken keys with cork.
619.ch: Clarinet fingering and the Tio family
619.q: Well you see. I always had an Albert system. Always used Albert. Yeah I always used an Albert system. See they only got one C sharp key on there. You see.

619.t: Tio's patched-up clarinet and the trip to New York
619.s: His wife is introduced; Laurent recalls a great clarinetist whose clarinet was held with rubber bands and cork and who was told to buy a new one before a New York trip.
619.ch: Clarinet fingering and the Tio family
619.q: And he used to play everything for the soul. The only time he got it, they made him get a new clarinet. That's when Peter Arm made his first trip to New York. Peter Arm said, you ought to be shamed. Man, he had rubber bands from top to bottom and cork shoving them holes from top to bottom. You…

619.t: Big Eye Louis and the C versus B flat clarinet
619.s: Big Eye played C clarinet most of his life and mastered it better than B flat, though local players mostly used B flat and E flat.
619.ch: Clarinetists, brass bands and the day job
619.q: Yeah. He just started playing the B flat in the late years, around in the Friday like that. Yeah, he used to play C clarinet, Big Illo. That's how Piku played with me, because Piku was playing alto. And the clarinet and I was playing clarinet soprano.

619.t: Picou's clarinets and Laurent's own clarinets with rings
619.s: They compare Picou's straight wooden clarinet with the ring-less and ring-equipped clarinets Laurent has owned and kept.
619.q: No. No. No, he got that. I had a couple of pieces of his second clarinet that he had. It was a sort of a tan wood in between the black. Oh yeah, I know. It was striped. Yeah. Straight horn like this. I had the bell, the mouthpiece, and the music stand that goes on. I had that from his voices. I can…

619.t: Valette clarinet and the instruments he sold
619.s: He shows a Paris-made Valette clarinet, describes his decorated clarinet that Willie Humphrey wanted, and the pencil model he sold.
619.q: I used to play opera and everything. You see the clarinet I told you I saw before this, that pentamon? You know who was running behind me for that clarinet? Willie Humphrey. Right now playing in the glass. He was running me down for that clarinet. Man, I had another one. I had another one before…

619.s: He explains the reed strengths he now uses and how he keeps his upper lip even with the teeth with pressure on the lip.
619.q: Oh, right now, you see, I used to use a three when I was playing regular. But the way I catch this thing now, my lips get so soft, I got to use a two, two and a half. Yeah. Sometime I use a three. If I'm playing kind of regular, every other day I can play a three, a three. But if I'm not, I might…

619.t: Laurent tries to play a number
619.s: Laurent attempts to play a number on the clarinet, tires, and mentions the many orchestrations he kept by the piano.
619.q: . . . . . I had them set on top of the piano, over 300-400 orchestration. And I could sit down and pick up the introduction on them numbers when I was playing every night. Pick up the introduction.

505.t: Giving up tenor for soprano: escaping Coltrane and the recipe
505.s: Around 1980-81 he stopped playing tenor to escape Coltrane and the formula of tenor for blowing, soprano for fusion, flute for ethnic.
505.q: Basically to escape Coltrane, in the end, although not the immediate reason. The deep-seeded reason, certainly. But I could have said that in 1973. So why then? It’s part of this midlife thing too. It’s all around me, 35 years old, whatever. It’s not midlife, but for me it was. I felt like I had a…

505.t: Doubling too thin; why soprano felt natural
505.s: Spread across three horns he was not mastering any; soprano felt physically natural and carried Miles's trumpet ideas.
505.q: bands, with Quest. I’m playing 15, 20 minutes of man time with my horn in my mouth, and I’m splitting it with three instruments. That’s five minutes per instrument. You can’t warm up. You don’t even get the reed wet. It dries out by the time you pick it up. Plus you got to put your reed. You got to…

505.t: Dropping flute, copyists of his tenor language, and returning to tenor
505.s: Imitators of his tenor language bothered him; soprano improved within two years, and he picked tenor up again around age fifty.
505.q: The other real practical reason was, there was a lot less water under the bridge for soprano in 1980. The tenor, still nobody was better than what I heard. There was just too many tenor players. Not contemporary. Just, I couldn’t escape Trane. It was enough to say – if I said Trane and Sonny, I…

505.t: Sopranino, G soprano and soprano pitfalls
505.s: Kirchner and Liebman compare sopranino and lower-pitched sopranos and mouthpieces, with a joke about the altissimo.
505.q: That’s the other thing. I’m not. Joe got a G soprano, the guy in Copenhagen. It’s handmade. It’s down to G. It’s long. It looks like a manzello/stritch, whichever one. Rahsaan had one that curved up.

505.t: Why people hate the soprano saxophone
505.s: Liebman agrees the soprano is high and annoying, hard to play in tune, and even Max Gordon disliked it.
505.q: Because it’s so high and annoying. It’s like darts in your head. And it’s also played by – it’s played badly, more readily played badly, because it’s a secondary instrument, which is one of the reasons why I didn’t want it to be like that. I don’t think I was that bad, but I didn’t want it to be…

505.t: Soprano's difficulty, doubling, and the advantage of its register
505.s: Most soprano players play it badly because of doubling; Liebman says its register matches the piano and cuts through.
505.q: That could be. But then you had Sidney Bechet, because there’s a big gap between Bechet and Lacy and Trane. They weren’t brought up on it. It’s true. It’s just a weird instrument to have. But again, it’s difficult, and most people that play it, don’t play it well, because it’s difficult and because…

505.t: Curved sopranos and Jan Garbarek's sound
505.s: Both dislike curved sopranos, though Liebman admires Garbarek, whose stark declarative style fits his sound.
505.q: Definitely trumpet. It’s something about a straight horn. See, that’s the thing. There’s a difference between a thing that curves. Even the curved soprano I don’t like as much. There’s something about that versus that.

185.t: Lorenzo's clarinets: ebony, keys and his family of clarinets
185.s: Tio describes his brother's ebony clarinet with open keys and trill keys, his A, B-flat, C, E-flat and D clarinets, and a bassoon played at Tranchina's.
185.q: Well, the instrument in them days, like, they didn't have as many keys, that is, metal keys, as the instrument of today. A hundred percent of that was open keys, you know, few metal keys.

185.t: Reeds, homemade pads and the broken key at the funeral
185.s: Lorenzo preferred hard reeds he trimmed himself and carried a needle and thread to make pads; Tio tells how a broken key at a funeral turned into a trill that moved the crowd.
185.q: Well, I think that his reed on his instrument was mostly a hard reed because when he'd buy a reed out of the stove, he'd eventually always stick it to his mouthpiece and try it out. And he'd loosen the clip and stick another old reed underneath it and probably eat it, sand it down to the end and…

185.t: Embouchure and teeth position on the mouthpiece
185.s: Russell asks about embouchure; Tio says Lorenzo pressed on his upper teeth without biting, and his father and uncle taught pupils not to bite, keeping the tongue free.
185.q: No, my brother had a way of his upper teeth. He would bite onto the mouthpiece? Upper teeth. Well, he had pressure against his upper teeth. In other words, he played clarinet so long that his teeth had been ground down in the shape of a mouthpiece. Mm-hmm. But for his biting on the lower teeth, no…

185.s: Lorenzo carved and trimmed his mouthpieces with a pocket knife, since players then had only the mouthpiece that came with the instrument.
185.q: his mouthpiece to suit himself oh yeah very definitely he had he had a pocket knife and if he he had a certain immature that to fit his mouth that's one thing he had he he if he had a new image of his mouthpiece he had to fit it to fit his mouth he had that's one thing you have to do better words…

185.t: Lorenzo's saxophones and the imported transposition book
185.s: Lorenzo took up saxophone around the First World War, first on an old brass horn, later owning tenor and a straight E-flat soprano; the family's imported French transposition book is probably in New York.
185.q: well i'll tell you he did play a saxophone uh about the first world war and that was an old brass saxophone that thing was green yeah well i remember him playing that but who it belonged to i wouldn't know i know it didn't belong to him but i know that after he began uh after saxophone began…
