128.q: I remember once they came on the labor's day and play the parade. Play the parade on the labor's day. Uh huh. And I was young for the day, you know. I couldn't come to town myself. I was looking. All the grown people, they came, you know. Uh huh.

594.t: His King Super 20 horn and Cannonball's switch to Selmer
594.s: He shows his King horn, which Parker and Cannonball played, and they agree the tone changed when Cannonball switched to Selmer.
594.ch: The King horn and closing views
594.q: Isn’t that something, because I did too. And so you really do know. Because that’s a subtle thing, but it is a difference. And I remember it as a CD or record, whatever, where he did play Selmer for a while. And it was great, and it’s still great ‘cause he’s great. And I remember that oh this is…

594.t: Talking saxophones: Selmer, King and Rowe's Buffet
594.s: They compare their horns, his Selmer VI and a King Super 20, and Rowe's old Buffet with its patina.
594.q: Now wait a minute because was it the record date because I played at Smokes twice, the record date it was on a Selmer VI and then I appeared at Smoke, maybe a year later, and it was a King Super 20.

594.t: The horn's warmth and articulation of Bird and Cannonball
594.s: Tape change, then more on the King's warmth and the special articulation of Parker and Cannonball.
594.ch: The King horn and closing views
594.q: Did you get enough shots with the horn here or should I keep it out? Okay, I’m going to put it back. But that’s interesting that you hear that difference, that Cannonball and that Selmer. That’s really something.

230.t: From alto to tenor to soprano
230.s: He moved from C melody to alto, then tenor after hearing Coleman Hawkins, and first played soprano in a school band.
230.q: First I got an alto, and I fiddled around with that, and then I heard Coleman Hawkins, and I said, "Oh, I've got to play the tenor," and so I got myself a tenor.

230.s: He seldom played clarinet, disliked it, and used it only for effects.
230.ch: Sidemen, mixed bands, the Apollo and Lena Horne
230.q: Oh, I very seldom used the clarinet. I did on one record, "Lament For A Lost Love," but not as a -- I didn't play any solos. I played -- they had the traditional

230.t: Buying his first soprano for Billy May's arrangement
230.s: He never owned a soprano until Billy May brought in a soprano part around 1939-40; before that only Hodges and Bechet played it.
230.q: a soprano part, and I said, "I haven't got a soprano, Billy." And he said, "Well, go buy one, the part's here." And I did.

145.t: Why clarinet has fallen out of use
145.s: Royal's views on the clarinet as a difficult instrument that modern saxophonists avoid in favor of flute.
145.ch: Violin, clarinet and the family name
145.q: Yeah, I liked it very much. The clarinet is a challenging instrument. As a matter of fact, the clarinet today is the bugaboo of most all reed players. They look at it and just cringe when they see a clarinet. They're very, very

145.t: Why the alto took over; no future as a black violinist; Eddie South
145.s: Alto was commercial; there were few opportunities for black violinists; Eddie South asked him to join in 1934; he no longer plays violin.
145.q: Well, it became that because it was the most commercial. So, you always have to follow the dollar sign wherever it goes, if you want to survive and survival was always the name of the game. I would have loved to have been a very good violin player, but there was no survival for me as a violin…

145.t: Clarinet phased out of the Basie book
145.s: Only three Basie pieces used clarinet; he transposed the April in Paris eight bars for sax.
145.ch: Billie Holiday, Basie leadership and studio work
145.q: There's not a clarinet book in there. The only clarinet -- at the time that I left the band, there was three things in his book that had clarinet in it. One was -- the last one that was put in it was a thing called "Blues Inside Out," by Quincy Jones, which I played the clarinet on the record on…

452.t: Buying a bass clarinet and doubling in Hampton's band
452.s: Cobb bought a bass clarinet for $75 from a soldier, borrowed money from Gladys Hampton, and played it behind vocalists in Hampton's band.
452.q: Stanley, I haven't been off it since and don't intend to get off of it. That has been my bread and butter over a period of years and I've been in this business now about 47 years this year.

452.t: C melody versus tenor, and whether C melody has any jazz use
452.s: Cobb explains that moving from C melody to tenor was easy apart from the key; the Danceses ask about the C melody's sound and Kenny Davern, and he calls it a marching band horn.
452.q: ALL RIGHT, But that doesn't make any difference what your key instrument is, as long as it's an instrument that you can play in jazz.

452.t: Gladys buys Cobb the horn Lucky Thompson wanted
452.s: Gladys sends Cobb to Manning's to pick a used horn for $265, which turns out to be the one Lucky had chosen; Cobb also talks about his Selmer and Yamaha horns.
452.q: Gladys called me the next day. She said, Arnett, you need a horn, don't you? I said yes. She said, Go to Mannings and try that horn out and see if you like it. That's where Lucky was getting it. If you like it, call me up at home. Give my right hand to God.

235.t: Selmer horns since 1944 and changing horns every two years
235.s: He plays Selmers like Hawkins, Byas and Ben Webster, bought his first second-hand in 1944, and changes horns every two years; his current horn came from Paris.
235.q: Well, I've been playing the Selmer horn for..oh, since 1944. Because I found that the Selmer had the best tone quality, over the years. And then, of course, I was influenced by Coleman, he had one. And Don and Ben Webster, you know, they had Selmers. But I notice that the Selmer, the tone…

235.s: He experiments with mouthpieces, and over the years used Van Doren, Vibrator, wartime plastic and now Rico Royal number three reeds.
235.q: Yeah, in Paris. Yeah, I found that to be true. And then mouthpieces, you're always experimenting with mouthpieces and you hear something new and so you keep your ear out for something new and you try it and if it isn't what you been usin'...you don't like it as well as what you been usin'...then…

235.t: Moving from clarinet to tenor saxophone
235.s: He joined the band on tenor, compares clarinet and saxophone fingering and explains he chose tenor for its human-voice sound.
235.q: No, I entered the band playing tenor saxophone, you know. Yeah. Because, you know, "tenor part", you know, tenor solos, Hahahaha.

174.t: Reeds, mouthpieces and strengths he used
174.s: Dejan talks about the reeds he used, mainly a three, sometimes a three and a half or two and a half, and how soft versus stiff reeds affect the lip.
174.q: Well, I tell you, now I couldn't tell you which string he used, but he always told me, very seldom you catch two people using the sand and shredder reeds, they're like in the sandbag, and he said, very seldom, because sometimes he'd buy me a, I'd give him a little number two, and you'd have to make…

174.s: He first heard saxophone in Manuel Perez's brass band around 1919-20.
174.q: Well, no, no, no, it's like I tell you, when Manner Perez was a brass band, that's the first time that I heard the saxophone with the brass band, because he always used a saxophone. Yeah, I thought Alexander was playing alto, and like I told you before, Eddie Sherry was playing E-flat clatter,…

622.t: Jack Pettis and how the tenor saxophone came to Chicago
622.s: Ashcraft tells how Pettis bought a C-melody sax on armistice night, ended up on tenor, and probably influenced Bud Freeman.
622.ch: Tenor sax and the Austin boys
622.q: Yeah, as an office boy. In the corner of Adams and LaSalle, the old building's still up there. On armistice night, or rather on fake armistice night, if you remember, that came a week early, he and the other office boy got good and plastered. And they bought, each of them bought from Land and…

622.t: Saxophone as a new instrument; violinists turning to reeds
622.s: They talk about Paul Beesey, Weedhoff and the Six Brown Brothers, why saxophone was easy, and why violinists took up reeds.
622.ch: Tenor sax and the Austin boys
622.q: You know, the saxophone at that point was really a quite new instrument. I mean, it wasn't recognized by legitimate musicians at all. And I think the first impression any of us had of a saxophone came either from Weedhoff or from the Six Brown Brothers.

880.t: Having the first saxophone in New Orleans; dating the photo
880.s: He claims the first saxophone in New Orleans in 1914; the photo is dated five or six years before World War I.
880.q: David Jones. David Jones, he took alto. Melo phone, you know? Yes. Later on he picked up saxophone. Now I had the first saxophone in New Orleans. You had the first saxophone? First saxophone. I put on the bass saxophone. I had saxophone in 1914. They used to travel. They used to travel. They used…

880.t: Buying his saxophone while playing bass with Holmes
880.s: With Holmes's encouragement he bought an alto saxophone for fifty dollars and was soon playing it with the band; clarinet came first.
880.q: Well, I was playing bass with the same band, Professor Holmes. And he said, John, you have a man like you shouldn't be on the bass. I got a shell, see? And I got the shell, played the shell a while, and said, why don't you get your saxophone? I'll get you saxophone pretty cheap. So, a friend of…

621.t: Louis Keppard, Willie Humphrey and the Albert system
621.s: Chat about Louis Keppard and Willie Humphrey and Duhé's use of the Albert system clarinet.
621.q: Next time you get over, you can go to see him. But you can avoid that, because I'm going there pretty soon. I can use the phone, true Willie Humphrey. Yeah, yeah.

621.s: Plastic reeds, Albert and Boehm systems, tone coming from the lip, and advice on embouchure.
621.q: Yes, sir. You know, those are the old ten-cent reeds. We used to have them go two for a quarter, three for a quarter. Sometimes they get thick up in your shirt, and then you wouldn't have no reed to play, see? Yeah. And you have to get the nickel and put two nickels together to get it even, see?…

37.t: Whether the saxophone belongs in New Orleans-style jazz
37.s: Stomp Evans is named in a talk on the saxophone as a post-New Orleans instrument, and both agree a well-integrated sax belongs in a jazz band.
37.q: well that shows how much I know well I guess you're gonna have a very divided opinion there about about about people who like and dislike the saxophone in a jazz band I imagine there are a great many people today who revile the things have no business in a jazz band those will be your died in the…

37.t: Bass player Branson Knolling and care of clarinet reeds
37.s: After a brief closing, they return to a New Orleans bassist and Chace describes preparing reeds and his youthful obsession with a spitty tone.
37.q: bring him around we'll play with him oh yes it prevents warm-up troubles uh... the reed's got to be ready and has to be damp enough i wish i were an expert here i remember bill russell questioning omer simeon about the exact texture of his reed and everything uh... well when i was a kid i thought…

11.t: Army-issued Boehm clarinet versus his Albert system
11.s: Why he kept his larger-bore Albert clarinet, its volume next to George Lewis's band, and carrying two instruments in service.
11.q: Well, I noticed that so many clarinet players that I found in the albert and I looked at them, the boar in the albert is much larger than the boar in the bane clarinet. And there's more volume. I can get more volume. I can play just another clarinet player and you can't hardly hear them. Well,…

11.t: Examining his Buffet clarinet; keys and reeds
11.s: Looking at his Buffet Albert system clarinet, its keys, his third California instrument and his reed strengths.
11.q: And you look through it in the light, the bore that drilled the hole in there, see how big that hole. Oh, yeah, it's really a big bore. Well, it's much bigger than the buffet.

267.t: Albert system versus Boehm system clarinet
267.s: Ford explains the fingering and tone differences between the Albert and Boehm clarinet systems and which players use each.
267.q: The difference in the Albert system is the old original system, or Louis Cantrell plays the Albert system, Willie Humphrey plays it. The only ones that play the other, or George Lewis play the Albert system. The ones that, it's an improved system. The newer system is Boyum or it's improved. It's a…

267.t: Why he moved from clarinet to saxophone
267.s: Ford says the music of the time called for saxophone, Dixieland players could not make a living, and clarinet is a good foundation. His mother signed for his first alto.
267.q: The music was coming out for saxophone. The clarinet was like a thing of the past, you know. And the guys wanted to, I wanted to saxophone. And if you were just going to play clarinet it would have been more of a Dixieland. I would have had the more of a Dixieland. That's all. And there weren't too…

1014.t: Playing old tunes for her at home on his troubled clarinet
1014.s: In his final week he played long-forgotten compositions for her in the back room while struggling with clarinet repairs.
1014.q: fallen or the children got hold of it. I don't know what happened but he was having an awful lot of trouble with it. And I can remember in the back room many times he'd lay there trying to fix it himself and do the repair shop and it wasn't fixed to his liking. And we'd try to fix it and cork it up…

1014.t: What became of his clarinets and the special piece he kept
1014.s: Discussion of his surviving clarinets, one Bill Russell gave him, the Smithsonian and Jazz Museum, the one going to Japan, and a small clarinet part she keeps along with rosary and knife.
1014.q: No. One of his clarinets, the one he played, the last one he played, it's still... they're both in the back room. One Bill Russell gave him. And then there's one that he had purchased, I believe, in England. That's the one he had been playing with mostly. That was his favorite one.

40.t: Raymond Burke and his strange instruments
40.s: Zanco jammed with Raymond Burke outside his shop, and describes the homemade horns and clutter inside.
40.q: Well, that was before, Raymond played, I think while Joe was still here. Raymond, Raymond Burke played with the group. He hadn't played since I've been in the group, but I would like very much, you know, the opportunity to play with him, you know. I stopped over at Raymond's shop pretty regular and…

40.s: They play the melody once, then solos, then two final choruses; sometimes two clarinets, as Kid Rene's band did. Few bands still use banjo.
40.q: Well, uh, usually once, huh? That's, uh, yeah, we'll go through it. Most of the time once. Most of the time once, then, uh, each, uh, instrument will take his solo. Then, uh, we'll take two choruses at the end, see, knock it out in two choruses.

41.t: Dates of the photos and Rappolo's Albert-system clarinet
41.s: Russell asks dates; Mares dates Paul's picture to 1919 Chicago, and says Rappolo played a 13-key Albert system wooden clarinet. More photos of Fountain, Hogg, Boyd, Pecora.
41.q: Paul's was taken in 1919 in Chicago. The picture of George is probably 10 years old, probably goes back to 50. I took that picture myself. The picture of Rapp up here goes all the way back to the early 20s, probably 1920.

41.t: Sitting in, giving up clarinet, Rappolo's borrowed clarinet
41.s: Mares sat in around Chicago and Biloxi but never became good enough; he kept the Albert clarinet Rappolo used on two recordings.
41.q: Well, I used to go sit in with Charlie Cadela and Abby Bernstein at the halfway house and at the Paris Royal later when Abby played there.

873.t: The Fifth Ward school band and its instruments
873.s: Lawrence helped the school band get tenor and baritone horns, and says saxophones have replaced them.
873.q: You take, well, I mean, a school band, we have a school band at the Fifth Ward, and the, the superintendent, and the, well, we, I'm, I'm, well, they say good friend. We, I always do the, all the, the mechanic work, tractors and car, and then I begin to work in school, teaching for the school. Well,…

873.t: Alto, soprano and baritone saxophones in the band
873.s: Talk of which saxophones his son, Herbert Trish and Clarence Hall played.
873.q: He had a, he had a, what did he have? What do you call it, one of those big girls? He had a tenor, he played tenor, I think, Clarence.

272.t: Taking up soprano sax, then alto, while keeping the Albert clarinet
272.s: Asked about a 1919 photo, he explains he played Albert-system clarinet in the Army, then took up soprano sax after seeing one, later alto.
272.q: Yeah, there's two instruments that they tried to go with the B flats of sax, you know. Mm-hmm. The, uh, trumpet, really, the trumpet sax. They, uh, put that on the market, you know. Mm-hmm. And so forth. I stuck right to the...

272.t: Switching to Boehm clarinet after pressure from Picou
272.s: He changed early from the Albert to the Boehm system after an older clarinetist kept offering to teach him and urged him to switch.
272.q: Yeah. You want to drink, Big O? No, so I want to talk to him. And every time he got an opportunity done, he'd make me sit down and he wanted to teach me. He knew. I told him no. I said, Big O, I don't want to play that kind of thing. I said, it's nice. I appreciate all that, but I don't want to…

734.t: The Joe Gabriel band and learning saxophone
734.s: Music was slow two-four Dixieland time; the Joe Gabriel band with the Williams and Gabriel brothers got him a saxophone.
734.q: Oh, we had a wonderful band. See, Claiborne William and Joe Gabriel, see, his four brothers played with Joe Gabriel, you see. He was our band leader. And I played saxophone and clarinet. At least I learned how to play clarinet. So they thought I was so apt, they wanted to improve the band, so they…

734.s: He used his lips over his teeth; B-flat and A clarinet; transposing with McCurdy and violin retuning.
734.q: No, I don't, I don't remember how he did it. But I, I tried to figure out, you know, I had a B in the A clarinet. See, we used to get in and use it too, you know. Yes. Well, I couldn't, I couldn't transpose like, probably used to play with the Robichaud, what is his name again? McCurdy? McCurdy,…

288.t: Early saxophone players: Tio, Dutrey, John and Willie Joseph
288.s: They try to name the first New Orleans saxophonists and discuss Willie Joseph and Bab Frank.
288.q: Because you take a fellow like Louis, he never did play nothing but that clarinet. No, he wasn't. But you take Tio, Tio had a saxophone, take Sam Dutrae, this fellow there, he had a saxophone. And who else? Two or three.

288.s: Charles says bands used clarinet from 1909 to 1916 before saxophones came in.
288.q: yeah, that's right, because we used to use clarinet. And then the clarinet player took it. Then they double up on second clarinet. But the clarinet was the main one. All those bands was using when I went into the city of New Orleans, from 19, I'm sure from 1909 up until 1916, that's all they were…

291.t: Clarinet versus soprano sax in the big bands
291.s: He explains he put the clarinet down for soprano sax in Morton's band and played clarinet parts in Oliver's.
291.q: So I put it down completely and like handed it, I put it down and I picked up on soprano sax. I used to play that with the, in the place of clarinet in General Rowe Martin's band. But I played clarinet with King Oliver's band, but I didn't play it like I played on here. I just played the big…

291.t: Clarinet and saxophone, and the old Boehm clarinets
291.s: He played his brother's clarinet first but went public on saxophone, and returned to clarinet later, taking solos on soprano sax.
291.q: Well, actually I played the clarinet first because my brother had a clarinet. When I was a kid I used to play his clarinet around. But when I got to play before the public, it was, it was the saxophone. Yeah.

484.t: Opening and the Invincibles; Brownlee's orchestra members
484.s: Interview opens with name, place and date (Pensacola, 5 May 1961). Brownlee names Invincibles members and sidemen in his own orchestra, with stories of the sax section and a fired saxophonist.
484.q: invincible so well that that's going way back now for dates when you try to make an old man remember dates you you're doing pretty good now but it was way back before and there was Laura Manaf and Teddy Fontalou, Hod Farah, Red Mackey, I think Doc Suchon played a couple of times with us and I…

484.t: Reed players on the record: Geordie's sobbing sax and Shields
484.s: Who played tenor, clarinet and bass sax on the record, including Harold Geordie's sobbing saxophone chorus.
484.ch: Owls, Werlein's and the OK record
484.q: Oh, Harold Geordie. He played a sobbing saxophone on one side. Funny part about that was that I said sobbing. At that same time, or right after that, we called it a sobbing. I told Harold that I thought he played a sad saxophone on one side, and I might call it a sobbing saxophone chorus that he…

296.t: Clarinets, saxophones and baritone horns in the early bands
296.s: Clarinetist Giovanni, E-flat and B-flat clarinets, no saxophones, and the difficult baritone part.
296.q: The horn, they call it baritone. Oh, baritone, yeah. I got that. Baritone wasn't so much, you know? It was the baritone part very difficult, you know? Uh-huh. And they didn't bother with that much. Some of them, they had barit one or two playing.

296.t: Piccolo players and absence of accordions
296.s: Piccolo players such as Doc Monique were few; accordions were not used.
296.q: I'm thinking about the name. What's the name? Actually, it was Bad Frank. Was it Bad Frank? No. Doc Monique. You know Doc Monique? Doc Monique.

858.t: Baritone, alto in the street, and clarinet
858.s: He played only alto in the street, did not take to clarinet, and they discuss the shortage of clarinetists.
858.ch: Brass bands and the WPA band
858.q: Yes, very, never been that much. I don't know, for some reason, uh, I didn't like it. I was still in all that. I'd known there would have been such a demand for it. But now, you know, stuck with it.

858.t: Banjo players and the soprano saxophone
858.s: Another banjoist, Harold Dejan and the soprano sax, and the difficulty of clarinet.
858.q: I won't be telling him if you saw me. I'll write it down. Yes, he's a boy so friend that I am. I haven't played it to. And Warren Bennett was playing Town of the Lake Swan. He's over there too.

301.t: Father's last performance and his flute and saxophone
301.s: Last heard playing flute in a union ball band; he played piccolo flute, started on C melody sax then alto.
301.q: Well, he played flute too. I didn't know that. Yes, he did. The only flute player, piccolo, really, was Bab Frank that I ever heard of in the old days that he played flute and jazz. He played a regular, a long flute then.

301.t: Embouchure covering both lips and Albert vs Boehm system
301.s: Father's technique of covering the teeth, lip control, and why Dutre stayed on Albert system clarinet.
301.q: Well, my father taught me that way. I had to start that way. Do you still do that? No, I don't. You don't do that now? No. And after I got able to play some, he said, well, you don't have to cover each other teeth anymore.

833.t: A brass band of foreigners at St. Catherine's and the lost $27 clarinet
833.s: He talks of the big brass band of mostly foreigners who liked him, and of a clarinet he paid $27 for and lost in a repair shop.
833.ch: Clarinet and lessons with Jim Humphrey
833.q: Big brass band. Mostly all foreigners, you know, from Belize. Something like that, yeah. Belize. All foreigners. And they used to be sticky to me, you know. They used to like me. And they'd play so good in a clad tone. You know, I had a good clad in a clad tone. I put that clarinet in the shop and…

833.t: The make of his clarinet and a hard-rubber clarinet that cracked
833.s: Russell asks if it was a Buffet; Robinson recounts a fellow's rubber clarinet that broke at the joint after wiping it in the cold.
833.ch: Clarinet and lessons with Jim Humphrey
833.q: Yeah, it could be. Yeah, no, I never did notice the name on it. Yeah. Of course the name be on the barrel of it, you know. Yeah. I never did notice. I remember a fella had a clarinet. He bought it. And it was cold that night. We were re-oist. And when we got through there, we were putting them up,…

1007.t: Why the Albert system clarinet helps him
1007.s: The Albert fingering helps him get the Bechet and Simeon sounds. He composes in keys that suit it and did not own a good Albert clarinet until about 2000.
1007.ch: Coming to New Orleans and the clarinet tradition
1007.q: And I’m constantly looking for things that are specific to this fingering system. You know I compose just to almost make a point that the New Orleans style has to be done on the Albert system. There’s things that I’ll put in. I’ll put things in certain keys so that they just don’t sound the same on…

1007.t: Staying true to the style amid modern rhythm sections; Albert system and Cullum band
1007.s: He struggled with mismatched accompaniment and front-line partners and wanted to stay a New Orleans clarinetist regardless, as Armstrong did. He switched to the Albert system after leaving for San Antonio to play with the Jim Cullum Jazz Band.
1007.ch: Coming to New Orleans and the clarinet tradition
1007.q: I struggled with that. I still struggle with that. I mean there being a disparity. Not as much, I’ve kind of figured it out, but yeah it was really interesting to recognize that there was going to be a disparity, not with just the rhythm section and the accompaniment but even with the other…

604.s: DeFranco explains his sister's name for the clarinet and agrees with Rowe that it is among the hardest instruments, with too many mediocre jazz clarinetists.
604.q: I got that from my sister Maryanne. Maryanne always called it an agony pipe. She says that’s what it sounded like when I was practicing. And she was right. It’s the strangest instrument.

604.t: His clarinet equipment and the Hanon exercises
604.s: He lists his Bari mouthpiece, Denman reeds, metal barrel and Yamaha clarinet, and says Hanon exercises can be swung.
604.q: The odd looking barrel? Well let’s see from top to bottom this is my creation, this mouthpiece and it’s put out by Bari, they release it, Bari mouthpieces.

107.s: He started on alto and moved to tenor in college because the band had too many altos.
107.q: I started out as an alto saxophonist in my own, in the bands I played with in Cincinnati, the little bands, my own band in high school and up until about my second year of college. And I switched to tenor because we had an over abundance of alto players and we needed a tenor saxophonist, and so I…

107.s: Foster clarifies that after his instruments were stolen he borrowed saxophones, one from Al Cafagna.
107.q: I may have mislead you earlier when I said something about not having instruments. I played on borrowed instruments in Detroit after having had mine stolen. I was able to borrow an instrument almost immediately to play.

209.t: Becoming a multi-doubler: flute, oboe and NBC staff orchestra
209.s: Unable to get studio work at 30, he took up flute and oboe together and two years later won a staff job at NBC as oboe doubler. He ended up with a full set of flutes, English horn and clarinets.
209.q: Yeah, I played the clarinet and the saxophone, and by the time I was 30 I felt, having heard a lot of players, that I could play at a par with them, but I wasn’t getting any of the good work in town, the studio work. And I was trying to figure out why. So I decided maybe I’d do better if I became a…

209.t: The burden and pay of doubling
209.s: Contractors said to bring everything, so he carried about 13 instruments in his car and kept them all in playing shape. Doubling paid well in recording and film but less in live television.
209.q: Well the difficult part about choosing that direction was it was rare when you’d know — I started doing calls then after that. After I got my staff job, then I started doing a lot of other calls as well. And it was rare when you got a call that you knew what you were going to be expected of you.

657.s: Bronze Yanagisawa alto, old Meyer mouthpiece, JodyJazz tests, Rovner ligatures and reed choice.
657.q: Oh yeah. It’s a bronze Yanigasawa. Yeah the guy from the factory, I was in the store playing different horns and I just happened to like this one. And you remember, I don’t know if you remember the old Yanigasawa I had, I played a Yanigasawa all throughout high school and so I’ve always loved the…

657.t: Flying with the alto; soprano and tenor
657.s: Travels light with alto; has tried soprano and tenor.
657.q: Oh yeah. I usually fly out of Syracuse and get a connecting flight out of Syracuse usually and go out to California and New Orleans.

897.t: Plastic Conn clarinets and Kenny Davern
897.s: Davern told White about the plastic Conn 15; White uses it for parades, funerals and daily composing to save his wooden horns.

114.t: Thinking differently on alto, tenor, flute and clarinet
114.s: Each horn's sound puts him in a different mood, so he thinks differently on each.
114.q: Well, what I like to do is, is to be able to play everything that I play on one instrument, be able to play them on all of them, but what happens is, you know, music is sound.

67.t: Joining Albert Wynn's band on saxophone
67.s: In early 1926 he joined the Wynn band in Chicago, playing mostly saxophone though he thought his cornet better.
67.q: I had my cornet, but I didn't play too much of it -- I thought I played better cornet than I did sax, but I liked saxophone better.

67.t: Playing soprano sax in a clarinet style
67.s: He took soprano because he could not learn clarinet, playing fast Noone and Bigard runs, which audiences liked.
67.ch: Chicago clubs, entertainers and tent shows
67.q: Well, it was a very unusual instrument, but that was my first instrument and I thought I played it very well, in fact, everybody liked the way I played the soprano saxophone.

155.t: What attracted him to jazz; subtone clarinet

1016.t: Keeping his sound after leaving Maynard

931.t: Learning from Sinatra and Goodman; his instruments

890.s: He explains why the E flat clarinet carried over the band, and how 'High Society' was a test of ability, like 'Giant Steps' for Coltrane.

1025.t: The curved soprano saxophone, a 1924 Conn
